doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: From the Marine Corps to RCA in California
summary: Hank explains how he moved from the Marines and an engineering course into a small New York studio, then west to Armed Forces Radio, RCA and Lou Adler.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: What was it that sent you into this career? Was there some kind of moment?

Oh no, not at all. I’d served four years in the Marine Corps. I got out of the Marine Corps and I started taking an electronic course, an engineering course at Columbia University. I got a job as a pick-up job, I’d come in and pick up some slack in some small studio and that led me into that. Before long I had quit working in school and got a job in the studio, and that was the end of that. I’ve worked in a studio in New York. I didn’t like the cold weather after spending a couple of years in Korea. I wanted to move to California. And there was no job offers at all. Anyway I came to California and worked in some small studios and I finally got a job at A&M.
Was it rather like an apprenticeship? Then you learned your craft by sitting next to somebody else?

Yeah, no, no. There’s no — at that time — there’s now schools and stuff for engineering but at that time there was no school for engineering. I just happened to get a lucky job working at a small studio in New York. And that led me into some bigger jobs and then I decided to come to California. I didn’t have a job but I just had to get out of New York, it was getting too cold. After being in Korea for a couple of years I wanted to get to the sun. So I left and I worked at Armed Forces Radio when I came out. It was the only job I could get in California. And luckily I got a job at RCA and started my career at RCA. It was great. I was at RCA for about ten years. It was a good learning experience, it was wonderful. I made contact with a lot of great artists: Tom Scott and I got into Ode Records, and I worked for Lou Adler, which was great. Lou was a wonderful, wonderful producer along with so many others. But anyway I’ve worked with Lou and we did “Rhymes and Reasons,” “Fantasy,” and stuff with Carole King.
